My issue isn't the rejection, it's the radio silence on emails and phone calls/voicemails that was frustrating and unprofessional. The second involved altering a contract without my knowledge. Summarized, the company received MY incentive payment in January 2026; I was unaware. I found out through talking with the CT Greenbank that it had been paid out. After many attempts via email and phone calls/voicemails over several months, a check was finally written to me in June 2026. Very disappointed in the communication, hence 3 overall stars. Bottom line: excellent installer but beware of communication. [...] clean site, kept asking if I had questions (I always did). Things to know? You have to keep track of your configuration and ask questions so nothing gets forgotten (But, once I asked, EVERYTHING on my list got done, and they were courteous about each reminder/request). Parts of the process can be a little confusing - Dave, Walter, John, even the owner helped me to become more knowledgeable along the way. If something doesn't make sense, ask them to explain it again or watch some installation videos online. But taken as a whole, huge process, I really had no problems, and that's saying something, given how intricate a process this is. They did a great job coordinating with us and our contractor and cared about the esthetics of positioning and running the conduits. Rooftop solar is good for the environment but has a fraud issue The rooftop solar business is a big source of consumer complaints. Across the country, prosecutors are investigating sales practices and financing arrangements. Now the solar industry is working to repair its reputation.

### Climate

# Rooftop solar has a fraud problem. The industry is working to build back trust

By

Jeff Brady

A crew installs a solar array on the roof of a home in Frankfort, Ky. in 2023. The rooftop solar business has become a big source of consumer complaints. Now the industry is working to repair its reputation.

A crew installs a solar array on the roof of a home in Frankfort, Ky., in 2023.  Michael Conroy/AP  hide caption

 toggle caption [...] “There's not really one place for consumers to complain to,” says Jenifer Bosco, an attorney with the National Consumer Law Center. “If they do have a problem with solar companies, they can complain to the Federal Trade Commission. They might complain to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, they might complain to their state AG's office.”

That makes it difficult to identify the exact number of complaints against residential solar companies. But it’s clear the number of dissatisfied customers has increased faster than the industry’s healthy growth rate.

Loading... [...] Customer complaints against the country’s residential rooftop solar industry have increased dramatically in recent years. One-star ratings on Solar Reviews increased more than 1,000% since 2018. Across the country, prosecutors are investigating high-pressure sales tactics and misleading financing arrangements. Some customers say they were victims of fraud and forgery. This threatens rooftop solar’s impressive momentum. Now, some solar companies are working to repair the industry’s reputation.
